speechtext:
I hope the parliamentary assistant will do more than answer the question. I hope he will implement his categorical assurance given the other night, by moving an amendment to put at least that much information into the proposed statute.
I want to say a bit more, Mr. Speaker, about the lack of information contained in the bill. While I share the views expressed by the member for Eglinton about the way in which this practice disregards the rights of parliament, I want to speak more particularly from the standpoint of the average citizen, be he a tenant or a landlord, who has a problem in the field of rent control. In a democracy it should be possible for a citizen who has to deal with a government department, or a government official, to be shown in black and white, and in simple language, what the law is. It should be possible to set before him a simple document telling him what his rights are. What a time any citizen, be he landlord or tenant, has today trying to find out what his rights are under this rent control legislation. As a matter of fact, as a result of the inadequate information that is available, many of these people write to their member of parliament for information. I think I know my way around the statutes, orders in council, regulations, documents, and the tremendous amount of material and information available to us here in Ottawa. I confess, however, that many of the questions that come to me in the field of rent control are presented in such a way that the only thing I can do is address a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
For example, a few days ago I had an inquiry about the present situation with respect to evictions. I knew there was something about that somewhere in the regulations, but it seemed to me a waste of time to
Transitional Measures Act try to find it, because I realized that if I did find it, it would probably have been amended since the time my copy of the regulations was issued. So I wrote to the Minister of Finance, and asked him if he would supply me with the latest office consolidation of the relevant orders, and in particular give me information so that I could answer the question I had received about evictions. I received a letter from the Minister of Finance dated March 22, 1950. I should like to read part of it:
There are no regulations dealing exclusively with evictions, but I would refer you to section 2 and section 13 of board order 800. Section 2 lists the types of property and leases not affected by that order and section 13 tells the circumstances under which a landlord may recover possession in accordance with the law of the province in which the accommodation is situated. In addition to these two sections, subsection 3 of section 4 of order 813 provides "that a landlord of any lodging as distinguished from a self-contained dwelling may recover possession by giving to the tenant a six-months' notice to vacate", and section 7 of the same order provides "that a landlord of any self-contained dwelling may give to the tenant a six-months' notice to vacate if he needs the accommodation as a residence for himself and the members of his family."
Yours very truly,
D. C. Abbott
I proceeded to look up, in the two booklets which the minister sent along with that letter, the various orders, sections and subsections to which he referred me. I found I was right in my original thought, that it would have been useless for me to look it up, because several of those sections had been amended. Little bits of paper containing the amendments had been pasted in the booklet, or the changes had been written in in ink.
My whole point, Mr. Speaker, in presenting this example, is that in addition to the affront to parliament that this sort of procedure involves, it is unfair to the average citizen of this country, because he is not able to go into a government office and be shown a clear statement of his rights. He should be able to find it in the law of the land. One should be able to turn up a statute governing the matter in question, and find it there. If he turns up what we have before us tonight, Bill 56, he finds it has one section, which changes the expiry date of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, so that it will continue in effect until April 30, 1951. That is all there is to it, and it tells him nothing. If, perchance, the parliamentary assistant decided it might be a good idea this time to keep the promise he made the other day, and put a schedule in the bill containing the information he said would be in a schedule to the bill, what would we then have in this 55946-821

Transitional Measures Act legislation? We would have, as the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said the other day, a book of numbers.
There would be two sections to that schedule. I am basing this assumption on what the parliamentary assistant said, as recorded at page 1106 of Hansard of March 24, 1950. The first section would list those orders in council that are being continued until April 30, 1951. We would know that the first one was P.C. 8528 1/11/41, wartime prices and trade regulations. Under that, we have a list of 15 other orders in council by number and date. The effect of these orders in council is simply to amend the first one. Then, the second order in council would be P.C. 9029 21/11/41, wartime leasehold regulations. Then, there is a list of nine more orders in council which amend that one, listed by number and by date. I shall not bother with the other four groups under that first heading, having to do with the orders in council to be continued in force, because they deal with relatively minor matters, nor with the second group of six orders in council, which will be discontinued as at March 31 of this year.
The main question before us is the continuation of rent control. As I say, in order to do that, there are to be these many orders in council carried forward. I suppose the parliamentary assistant is thinking of saying that it would be ridiculous to include, as a schedule to the bill, all of those 26 orders in council to which I have referred. In speaking of 26, I mean P.C. 8528, plus its 15 amending orders, which, taken together, constitute the wartime prices and trade regulations; and then P.C. 9029, which is the wartime leasehold regulations, plus its 9 amending orders in council. One of the reasons that it would be ridiculous to carry all of those orders in council forward into a schedule is that most of them are now dead. As a matter of fact some of the material the member for Eglinton was reading here tonight, and complaining about, is a dead letter. He was worked up over some of the authority that seemed to be contained in them, but rather needlessly, I would say.
The member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) seems to be enjoying the fact that I am saying that about the member for Eglinton. I tell him, however, that if it is the case that most of those 26 orders in council are in the category of dead letters, would it not be a simple matter to boil them down to a few sections in the statute itself that would give the necessary authority for rent control? Would it not be a simple matter to put these regulations down in black and white in the statute so that people of this country would know what their rights are? Let me come back to my point. The whole


purpose of the first sixteen orders in council referred to in this schedule, which the parliamentary assistant said would be in the bill but which is not in the bill, is simply to keep alive on paper the wartime prices and trade regulations as a base or an authority for there being a rent control division. Let us get rid of all that and simply enact, by one section of the bill, the rent control authority. Similarly, P.C. 9029 and its nine amending orders in council simply make various changes in the original constitution of the rent control authority, all of which could be boiled down and made clear.
A while ago I referred to the documents which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) sent me the other day. One of them is entitled:
Office Consolidation May, 1949
Wartime Prices and Trade Board Orders Respecting Maximum Rentals and Termination of Leases for Housing Accommodation and Shared Accommodation
When I look into the booklet I find that within the space of seven pages there is printed P.C. 9029 as amended by the nine amending orders in council referred to as item 2 in the promised schedule. Right there that suggests the possibility of boiling all this material, which it is quite hard to find, down to a fairly simple statement. The parliamentary assistant says, "Oh, you need the other orders in council in order to give authority to P.C. 9029". This parliament now has authority to constitute or to continue its constitution, if you will, the rent control authority that is in existence; and I submit that it is something of that kind that should be done.
Then after you get this P.C. 9029 by this devious process of carrying forward the whole raft of dead-letter orders in council, you then move on to the board orders; and their numbers, of course, run fairly high. I have reached as high as board order No. 813; but they do not all relate to rent control. Many of them, of course, dovetail into each other. Any time that a difficult question is put to the Minister of Finance or to the rent control people, they have to get the answer. They have to sit down and study this section and that, and make sure that one section has not been repealed by another. Would it not be a great deal simpler-in fact, would it not save time and labour for all of the people out in the various offices-if once and for all the whole business were boiled down to a simple statement?
I argue that point for the sake of efficiency and because I think it is unfair to ask parlia-

ment to pass legislation that is so involved as this is and is so far removed from parliamentary investigation or inquiry. I urge it also because it seems to me that the democratic tradition is a good one, namely, that the people of the country have the right to know what the law of the land is and have the right to know what their rights are. As the situation is now, any citizen, whether landlord or tenant, who goes into a rent control office is obliged to take the word of the official that he is telling him what his rights are or are not. One of the reasons that we get many letters from these people is not that they do not trust the official who is behind the counter in the rent control office but that they have been brought up in the tradition that citizens in a democratic society have a right to know what the law is.

speechtext:
Quite so. The official probably does what I do; he writes a letter to Ottawa, to the Minister of Finance, and gets a reply referring him to all these various sections, and gets a new book with the little slips pasted in so that he is brought up to date. Surely it is a fundamental rule that our citizens are entitled to know what the law is. When they go into a government office in Winnipeg or Vancouver it should be possible for them to see the law in black and white. They should know whether they are being given justice or not, and whether the law is being interpreted rightly or not. They should know when and where they may go to court to have their rights under the law protected, if they wish to do so.
I submit that it is not a good enough excuse simply to say that there are only thirteen more months with this and let us muddle along with it as it is. We have done far too much of that already, particularly since the war, with the habit that the government got into; and in my view this would be a good place to begin with the enacting of proper legislation.
One other comment I should like to make at this time is this. I suppose we have to accept the government's statement in the matter, a statement which is being carried forward into the bill, and that is that it is definitely going out of the field of rent control thirteen months from now. All previous extensions of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act have carried with them the possibility of that act being continued for another year by the simple device of a resolution of both houses of parliament. For the first time that device is not being included, and we have a bill which foreshadows a definite ending of rent control at the end of
Transitional Measures Act April, 1951. As I say, the people in my city of Winnipeg and in other cities across the country have had, in the last few years, so many hard knocks in the matter of rent control that they have become inured to the government's callousness; but I would not be doing my duty if I did not again protest the way in which we have had, not rent control, not protection of the interests of our people, but rent decontrol hastened or pushed forward at an unnecessary rate, particularly in view of the failure of the government to deal with the fundamental problem in this field, namely, the problem of decent and adequate housing for all our people.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
With the purpose of this act, Mr. Speaker, in so far as it relates to a measure of rent control, there is not much disagreement in this house. But there should be disagreement on the part of every member of this house with the procedure that is being followed if he really examines what this act does and what result is produced. As has been pointed out, there is a problem presented to the members in connection with this present act which proposes to continue the transitional powers for another thirteen months,, by the simple fact that this is March 28 and that, according to the information conveyed to the government by the law officers of the' crown, this and any similar act terminates at midnight the day after tomorrow. For that reason we are confronted with a situation in which, if we assert the position that should be asserted in regard to legislation of this kind, we can produce a situation in which there would be no remaining rent control, simply because of the dilatory conduct of the government and their failure to bring this legislation before the house in time for hon. members to have the opportunity of giving it ample consideration and of finding some alternative course.
Now, from the remarks that have already been made, I wonder how many hon. members realize exactly what they are being called upon to pass. Do members of this House of Commons realize-those of them who are showing sufficient concern to listen to this debate on this tremendously important bill- that what is now being sought is the power to continue not only price controls, but a very wide measure of control, not only over goodsy but over services? And do they realize that under this act as presented, if it is passed by the House of Commons, the government could deal with human services in any way it might see fit, and without any limitation imposed by the act?
You may say that would not be done. Other things have been done by this government which have greatly surprised members erf the

Transitional Measures Act house, as well as the people of Canada generally. I think a number of members have either misunderstood or misread the undertakings given by the government as to the scope of the continuing powers. I think many members of the house thought that it dealt only with rent controls.
I propose to speak about rent control, under this unsatisfactory method; but I also propose to speak of the other powers that are continuing. If this unsatisfactory method, this utterly unsound method of dealing with this particular problem, is to be adopted-and the very casual manner in which the government brings this on at the last moment would seem to make that almost a necessity-then it is quite true that it was necessary to continue the existence of the board which supervises the rent control provisions. That board is the board set up separately under order 8528, which was the original order in council establishing the wartime price and trade regulations. That order created the wartime prices and trade board, which is the board referred to in the rent control provisions.
Therefore in order to make the rent control provisions effective, without any change, and carry those loose provisions forward, it was necessary to provide for the continuance of this board. But they have gone a great deal farther than that, to provide for the continuance of the board. They have continued in force all the regulations that were put into effect, except those that were definitely limited in March of 1949.
Again may I say that a great many hon. members did not fully appreciate the effect of the provisions of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, which was discussed last year. Section 2 of that act reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in the said act or in any order or regulation set out in the schedule thereto, the wartime prices and trade board shall not
(a)	exercise any of its powers under paragraph (f) of subsection one of section four of the wartime prices and trade regulations; or
(b)	grant leave to prosecute any person for violation of subsection one of section eight of the wartime prices and trade regulations;
with respect to any goods or services other than the goods and services with respect to which an order of the board was made under that paragraph and is in force at the commencement of this act.
Now, paragraph (f) of section 4 is the part of section 4 which relates to the fixing of certain maximum or minimum prices on certain goods, and relates only to the power of the board in relation to those. But it does not in any way limit the power of the board to deal with a great many other very important subjects. It does not in any way limit the power of the board to deal with everything from (a) right down to (m) of the powers that were originally conferred.

Then when you come to section 8 (1) with respect to the wartime trade board we find that section 8 is the one which relates to offences, penalties and prosecutions, and that the only subsection of section 8 which has been deleted is the subsection which refers to penalties for goods being sold at higher than a reasonable and just price. But it does not in any way remove any of the other penalties in relation to orders made by the board in regard to prices, or the control of goods or services.
Now, this is not simply an exercise in the definition of terms. Just let us see some of the things that are being continued by this bill that is now before us. I shall take only a few of them, to illustrate the extent of the powers that are being continued by this bill now under consideration. Let us take paragraph (g), for instance, of section 4 (1), which provides that the board shall have power-
To prescribe the terms and conditions upon which, and the manner and circumstances in which, any goods or services may be produced, manufactured, extracted, refined, processed, stored, transported, purchased, sold, offered for sale, supplied, assembled, installed, constructed, distributed, exhibited, advertised, delivered, used or dealt in or with, either generally or by specified persons, and to prohibit transactions and acts not in accordance therewith.
Mr. Speaker, that practically gives this board power over every human activity in this country, either in dealing with goods, or in offering their services. This provides power in the hands of this government for the conscription of manpower under any terms they see fit.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am pleased to note that the very capable lawyer who has just spoken realizes that these are in force. I am happy that he has enlightened the parliamentary assistant to that extent. When he asks whether it would do any harm to have them still in force I would remind the hon. member that these orders were put into effect in the days of great emergency just after the outbreak of war. They granted powers that were justified and would have been accepted by the people of Canada only under those grave conditions. There is no occasion eleven years afterward for an hon. member to say, "You have had them for eleven years, you might just as well continue them." The fact is that on other occasions this government has revived statutes or powers that were available to them without notice to this House of Commons and to the parliament of Canada.

Transitional Measures Act
I for one do not believe that any hon. member of this house should let pass in this casual way powers of this kind that place in the hands of the government, at their whim at any time, full control over all business and personal activities of this country and full power over the personal services of our people, in whatever capacity those services may be performed. Yet that is what is before us. Let us see what the Minister of Finance said with regard to the exercise of these powers. He is reported at page 1089 of Hansard of March 24, 1950, as having said:
The government does not intend to invoke the limited powers now granted by the act to reimpose controls already lifted.
That is no assurance that these powers will not be invoked. It simply says that the government does not intend to invoke. There are hon. members of this house who have been here for many years and who will recall occasions on which this government explained originally that they did not intend to do something but, finding they had authority and power to do it, felt that it was appropriate and necessary for them to exercise that power. This is only a declaration of intention and nothing more.
If the government has no intention of using these powers, then let them by order in council repeal tomorrow that part of order 8528 which does not relate to the mere creation of the board which is necessary for the purposes of carrying on the rent controls under order 9029. If they do that they will give evidence that they have no intention of exercising any wider powers. If they do not do that then every hon. member here must accept full responsibility for leaving powers in the hands of the government under which in time of any measure of stress powers and controls inconsistent with our system of parliamentary responsibility may be invoked.
I am going to leave my remarks as to these wide provisions at this time in the hope that between now and three o'clock tomorrow afternoon the government will recognize it has no occasion to continue such powers unless it has some intention not disclosed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). There is one simple way to demonstrate that, by passing the appropriate order in council which they can do in a matter of a few minutes with the knowledge before them. I am simply saying that for the time being I am going to leave the discussion of this particular subject so that the government will have an opportunity to consider the matter before the debate is revived tomorrow afternoon.
I will pass on to the provisions as to rent control. I have made our position clear on an earlier occasion. For the purpose of keep-

ing the record quite straight I propose to refer to the position we took last year when these same measures were before the house. I do so because of the misinterpretation which has been placed upon the position which we took. On March 14, 1949, in the discussion of these very same measures, I had this to say, as reported at page 1449 of Hansard for that date:
I would recall again that when the government of Canada asks us to give these loose powers to deal with rent control, with steel control, with timber control, with priorities, and with ail these other controls, it has already said to the provincial governments, in effect: We do not believe that there is any emergency of the kind which necessitates our general authority; you go ahead and deal with these orders and we shall be very happy to leave the matter with you. Of course, the provinces will be called upon to deal with these by statute, and if they could deal with a rent control act, defining the rights of the tenants and landlords, then this house could have an act by which they could deal with other matters in the same way. And we should have them. There is no difficulty whatever in having proper acts of parliament to deal with each one of these subjects, which will restore to parliament its own authority, and which will restore to the members elected by the people of Canada their opportunity to say what the rights of the people will really be.
Further down on the same page I had this to say:
If the Canadian parliament has any right to conn tinue these powers, then it has the right and the authority to deal in the proper way with every one of the subjects covered in this omnibus bill; and that is the proper way to deal with it. But do not ask this House of Commons, do not ask parliament, to pass this omnibus bill which puts in one package all these loose and arbitrary powers in the way this one does.
The continuance of these powers involves an extremely wide and arbitrary measure which permits ministers of the crown, and appointed officials who delegate their authority to others, powers which are not defined and which are expressly made free from the ordinary restraints of the courts; and they become in effect a sort of arbitrary power which we have come to associate with dictatorships in other countries.
I deal further with the same subject at page 1454 of Hansard for the same date in these words:
I urge hon. members on both sides of the house, particularly those members on the other side of the house who have themselves criticized bureaucracy and the petty czars and dictators, that they vote against this resolution. By doing so they will insist upon proper acts being brought forward and they will also insist upon the return of true democratic parliamentary procedure in Canada.
The matter came up for discussion again on March 16, 1949, and on that occasion I was again discussing the question of dealing with these matters at that stage by loose orders instead of by clearly defined statutes which would leave no doubt about the rights of those affected by the legislation. I wish

to quote these words from what I said on March 16, 1949, as reported at page 1545 of Hansard:
I said before and I repeat that the government still has the opportunity to deal with this ini the parliamentary way. Bring before this house a rent control bill that will really deal with the rights of tenants and! the rights of landlords, and really establish the rights of our people generally; and the government will find support from every part of this house.
That was what I said in March of last year and it is what I say now. This is a subject which should be dealt with by a bill which will define the rights of those who are affected in such a way that from one end of the country to the other the rights of tenants and of landlords in their related capacities may be clearly determined, that they may be able to go to the courts to have decisions made in our ordinary constitutional way, and that they may be no longer subject to the arbitrary decisions of a board set up to meet the emergencies of war which has no place in this fifth year after the war in a free Canada.

The Budget-Appendix THE NATIONAL ACCOUNTS
National Income, Output and Expenditure
National Income measures the annual earnings of Canadian residents from productive operations. As such it includes salaries, wages and other forms of earnings by employees, in cash or otherwise, plus military pay and allowances. It includes corporation profits and other returns on invested capital. It includes the net income of farmers and of others who are in business on their own account.
Gross National Product is the value at market prices of all the goods and services produced in a year by the labour, capital and enterprise of Canadian residents. It is obtained by adding to National Income indirect taxes and such costs as depreciation allowances which may be regarded as entering into the cost of the goods and services produced, but do not form part of the incomes of Canadians. On the other hand, government subsidies, which reduce the price to the consumer or add to the income of producers, have to be deducted since they form part of the income of Canadians but do not enter into costs of production.
The goods and services produced in a year are either sold at home or abroad or added to inventories. Gross National Expenditure indicates how the Gross National Product was disposed of. Thus it measures the same total as Gross National Product but in a different way. Since foreign expenditures on Canadian goods and services, i.e., exports, form part of the earnings of Canadians in the Gross National Product, they are likewise included in Gross National Expenditure. While Canadian expenditure on imported goods and services is included in the totals of consumer expenditure, government expenditure and gross home investment, it is not part of the disposition of Canadian production and is therefore deducted.

Production and Income
The total value of goods and services produced by Canadians continued to rise during 1949, though at a lower rate than in the previous year. Eliminating the upward price change, it is estimated that national production in terms of physical volume increased by about 2% between 1948 and 1949.
Looking back to 1939, the national product has grown in value by over 180% and in physical terms by about 70%. Most of the increase in physical output occurred during the war years and can be attributed in large measure to the absorption of unemployed labour and resources. During the postwar years of high employment, output has shown a small but steady annual rise.
Income received in the form of wages and salaries rose by 7% between 1948 and 1949, reflecting the continued high level of employment and a further increase in rates of pay. Farm income, which has risen proportionately more than any part of the National Income since prewar years and which increased by about one-third from 1947 to 1948, fell by 5% between 1948 and 1949. Both lower prices and reduced crops account for the decline.
Investment income and the income of unincorporated businesses other than farming were up very slightly from the previous year.

On the other hand, transfer payments such as family allowances, old age pensions, veterans benefits and charitable contributions by corporations are included in arriving at the total of personal income.

Saving
For the purpose of the National Accounts, saving is defined as being equal to investment.
Thus, a balance sheet can be constructed showing, on the one side, the sums which Canadians do not spend out of their incomes on immediate consumption-which are defined as saving-and, on the other side, the total amount spent for non-consumption goods such as factories, machinery, houses, additions to inventories, etc.-which are defined as investment.
Saving can therefore be regarded as the source of funds out of which investment expenditure is financed or, alternatively, investment expenditure can be regarded as providing an outlet for the savings set aside out of income.
A surplus of government revenue over expenditure adds to the total of saving. It is in effect a form of community saving. A government deficit, on the other hand, is a claim upon, and therefore a deduction from, private saving.

Revenue and Expenditure of all Governments
In Table 10, "Government Transactions Related to the National Accounts", an attempt is made to bring together in one statement and under uniform headings the activities of all governments in Canada on a calendar year basis.
The table is designed to include only those transactions which have relevance for the National Accounts, and consequently the surpluses or deficits shown here do not agree with those shown in the various public accounts. It has been necessary to adjust the conventional accounting statements of fiscal year revenue and expenditure to exclude purely bookkeeping transactions as well as the purchase and sale of existing capital assets. Extra-budgetary funds such as unemployment insurance, workmen's compensation and pension funds have been added, and surpluses or deficits of Government enterprises are likewise included. In the federal accounts some of the more substantial adjustments are as follows: addition of national defence recoverable expenditure, allocation of war refunds to prior j'ears, adjustment of corporate taxes to an accrual basis, elimination of sales of war assets to business, and elimination of British Commonwealth Air Training Plan write-off from expenditure. In addition the federal figures have been adjusted to a calendar year basis by using the monthly figures published by the Comptroller of the Treasury. Government loans to foreign countries or accumulation of gold or foreign exchange are not included with government expenditure.
For purpose of analysis, expenditures by governments may be divided into two main categories: expenditures for the purchase of goods and services, and so-called transfer payments, i.e., family allowances, old age pensions, veterans benefits, the greater part of the interest on the public debt, etc., which do not arise from current production of goods and services. The first category represents the demands which governments place on the annual output of the nation Transfer payments, on the other hand, simply add to the sums available for [DOT] spending or saving by the recipient.

speechtext: The Budget-Appendix

When goods are exported (unless they are given away) they give rise to payments or debts in favour of Canada. Similarly, when goods are imported they give rise to payments or debts in favour of the rest of the world. Other transactions, such as interest and dividend payments, the tourist trade, freight and shipping charges, also give rise to similar payments or debts in either direction. The difference between the debits and credits arising from these current transactions is referred to as the net balance of international payments on current account. When total credits exceed total debits within a year, the rest of the world has gone into debt to Canada or Canada has paid off some of her debt to the rest of the world. When total debits exceed total credits, the net position is, of course, reversed.

Canada's net surplus on current account of $193 million in 1949 was $260 million less than in 1948. The change is split evenly between commodity trade and other current transactions. About $190 million of the change is the result of an increase in Canadian payments, very largely in payments to the United States, arising from increased imports from that country. The other $70 million of the change is the result of a decrease in Canadian receipts, chiefly in receipts from E.R.P. countries other than the United Kingdom, and resulted mainly from a reduction in exports to those countries. There was very little change from 1948 to 1949 in either the value of exports to or of imports from the countries of the sterling area (including the United Kingdom); consequently Canada's surplus on current account with the sterling area was substantially the same as in the previous year.
Compared with 1948 there were in 1949 considerably increased exports of wheat, newsprint, non-ferrous metals, and a few types of fully manufactured goods, and substantially reduced exports of other agricultural products, especially of meats, of most other forest products, and of manufactured goods generally. Export prices were slightly higher in 1949 than in 1948 and the volume of exports in 1949 was lower than in 1948 by some 3%.
An appreciable decline occurred in imports of coal and petroleum. Otherwise imports generally were higher, including large increases in fruits and vegetables and motor vehicles and parts. Import prices were slightly higher in 1949 and there appears to have been little change in the volume of imports.

Taking the year as a whole, price levels in Canada in 1949 were higher than in 1948. The year ended, however, with the indexes of both general wholesale prices and the cost of living several points below the postwar peak.
General wholesale prices reached their highest point in December 1948 at a level about double 1939. Subsequently there has been a decline of about 2%. The prices of Canadian farm products reached their peak somewhat earlier- in July of 1948-at a level more than two and a half times the 1939 average and have since declined by about 9%.
The decline in agricultural prices found its reflection in a decline in food prices to consumers, which form a high proportion of the items included in the cost-of-living index. As a result, in spite of rising rents, the cost-of-living index is now about 1% below its peak of August 1949. However, rent increases which took place under the recent changes in rentals regulations are not yet recorded in the official index.

2.	SUMMARY OF GOVERNMENTAL FINANCIAL OPERATIONS

2.	Total revenues of the Government for the year ending March 31, 1950, are now estimated at $2,548 million. Expenditures, on the other hand, are estimated at $2,437 million. On the basis of these figures it would appear that the Government's accounting or budgetary surplus for the current year will probably total something in the neighbourhood of $111 million compared with $595-5 million for the year ended March 31, 1949. As a result of the current year's estimated surplus of $111 million, the Government's net debt (i.e. the excess of total liabilities over total active assets) will reflect a reduction of an equivalent amount.
3.	In addition to collecting revenues and making expenditures in the narrow accounting or budgetary sense of those terms, the Government also receives and disburses substantial amounts of cash in other ways. These other receipts and disbursements relate to transactions which give rise to increases or decreases in the Government's assets and liabilities, and they do not, therefore, appear in what might be called the Government's income account for the year, nor do they enter into the calculation of the Government's annual surplus or deficit. In 1949-50 the total of these other disbursements exceeded the total of other receipts, and a large part of the cash provided by the 1949-50 surplus had to be used to finance the difference. The balance of cash available for the reduction of funded debt was, therefore, considerably reduced.
4.	The following summary shows the nature and extent of these nonincome account transactions and their effect upon the Government's net cash position. The figures indicate that although a total cash sum of $287 million became available to the Government as a result of the current year's budgetary surplus, this was reduced to an over-all "cash surplus" of only $67 million after financing the large cash requirements on non-income account.
